summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 11.2 percent of firms in transportation and warehousing reported using AI in the most recent reference period, up from 10.7 percent in the prior period. That measured figure almost certainly understates the sector's actual exposure, because AI is embedded in equipment and platform software that operators use without categorizing it as AI adoption, and the survey captures only direct firm-level use.

The most visible concentration of investment is in autonomous freight. Aurora describes a system it calls the Aurora Driver, built on verifiable AI and integrated into commercial truck platforms including the Volvo VNL Autonomous, with operational pilots hauling freight between Fort Worth and El Paso in partnership with carriers such as Werner. Partners quoted by Aurora point to safety and efficiency gains on long-haul routes, and the company cites millions of autonomous miles as evidence of consistent performance. The American Trucking Associations, which represents more than 37,000 member organizations, tracks the policy environment that will determine how broadly such systems can be deployed, including questions of licensing, liability, and federal recognition of Level 4 operations.

In fleet operations more broadly, Samsara reports that its AI-powered platform serves more than 20,000 operations and credits AI dashcams, real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching, and drowsiness detection with preventing more than 380,000 accidents. That figure is the clearest ROI-adjacent claim in the source material and comes from a company whose platform spans cameras, video AI, predictive analytics, equipment management, and driver coaching. C.H. Robinson, one of the largest third-party logistics providers, frames its AI deployment in terms of autonomous logistics orchestration, where its system analyzes, decides, executes, and improves continuously across shipments, covering load matching, routing, and supply chain management at scale.

Aviation and maritime are both advancing AI deployment under close regulatory oversight. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has published its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0, which sets out safety and ethical requirements, an action plan for conceptual guidance, and anticipated rulemaking, and states explicitly that it is a living document updated annually. Airbus describes a vision for a decarbonized, connected, and autonomous aerospace future and positions AI-driven digitized operations as central to realizing it. On the water, the International Maritime Organization adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, with the code entering into effect on 1 July 2026. The IMO notes that no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships currently operate autonomously or by remote control, but that successful trials have demonstrated feasibility and that such ships may enter commercial service in the near future. Wärtsilä, which describes itself as a global leader in marine and energy technologies, cites AI-driven predictive analytics as one of the tools it deploys in support of decarbonization goals for its marine customers.

Regulatory posture is the dominant constraint across all modes. EASA's roadmap governs what can fly commercially in European airspace, with nothing reaching passengers without certification. The IMO's MASS Code is currently voluntary but is designed to transition into a mandatory instrument, meaning operators and designers building toward autonomous shipping must already engage with its goal-based framework covering design, construction, operation, and certification. Waymo, which traces its lineage to the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and completed its first fully autonomous ride in 2015, publishes safety methodology and crash-rate comparisons that constitute the most complete public evidence base from a deployed autonomous vehicle operator, and explicitly frames autonomous driving technology as a safety intervention aligned with the U.S. Department of Transportation's National Roadway Safety Strategy.

A reader evaluating AI deployment in transportation should distinguish between the three layers of activity the sources describe. Telematics and fleet AI from platforms like Samsara are commercially available today at scale and carry documented safety and efficiency claims. Freight brokerage and logistics AI from operators like C.H. Robinson is similarly live, with AI embedded in core commercial workflows. Autonomous vehicles and vessels, by contrast, remain in varying stages of pilot, certification, or early commercial operation depending on the mode, with the regulatory timeline at EASA, the FAA, the IMO, and relevant national bodies setting the practical deployment horizon more than the technology itself.
